About: Polar vs Cartesian — One Motion, Two Descriptions

Source

Lecture
1 — Geometry
Simulation
Simulation 1 — Polar vs Cartesian (lecture visual aid)
Concept
Coordinates are labels we choose to describe the same physical motion — not the motion itself. Identical circular motion gives sinusoidal Cartesian traces but trivially constant/linear polar traces.
Serves
Use Cartesian and polar coordinates to describe points and trajectories; understand coordinates as labels rather than physical observables; geometry as a mathematical description of space.
Structural target
The intuition that complicated coordinate behaviour implies complicated motion — refuted because the same circle is two sinusoids in Cartesian yet r = const, θ = linear in polar.

Guided Inquiry

1 · One point, two sets of labels

Let’s meet our point. P travels a circle of radius R = 1 about the origin O at constant angular speed ω. You can write its position as a Cartesian pair (x, y) — distances along two perpendicular axes — or as a polar pair (r, θ) — the distance from O and the angle from the x-axis.

Take a look at the apparatus: the blue segment is x, the red segment is y, and the line running out to P is r at angle θ.

2 · Which description is simpler?

Nothing’s been plotted yet, so this one’s a pure prediction. For this circle, plotted against time, which pair of numbers do you think gives the simpler pair of curves?

3 · The number that never moves

Now watch the readouts. As P goes round, x and y each sweep from −1 to +1, yet r reads 1.000 throughout — at 45°, x = 0.707 and y = 0.707. So what do you think r really is?

Try raising ω: the Cartesian curves pack more cycles into the window and the θ ramp steepens, but r(t) stays flat at 1.

4 · A different path

Now we’ll change the path. Suppose P moved along a straight line at constant velocity instead, passing to one side of O. Which description do you think would give the simpler pair of curves then?

5 · Coordinates are a choice; geometry is not

Let’s look back at what stayed put. Through every card the distance from O held at 1.000, while both of its Cartesian labels swung across their whole range. A number that every coordinate system agrees on is called an invariant — and in special relativity, this same move, new labels with one agreed number, gives you the spacetime interval.

The Physics

Polar vs Cartesian · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A coordinate pair is a label for a point, not the point itself. This sim moves one point round a circle and writes its position two ways, so you can compare the curves each description draws.

What you'll learn

  • How one point is described by a Cartesian pair and by a polar pair.
  • How the two descriptions of the same motion compare as curves in time.
  • How ω sets the speed, the period and the number of turns in the plot window.
  • How to tell a property of the point from a property of the labels.
One point P, labelled two ways.

What's on screen

  • P (yellow dot) on a dashed circle of radius R = 1 about the centre O.
  • r (green line): the arm from O out to P, at angle θ from the +x axis.
  • x (blue) and y (red): dashed drops from P to the two axes.
  • Plots: x(t), y(t), r(t) and θ(t) against time, with a dot at the present instant.
  • Live Readouts: the current x, y, r and θ.
See itStart P from the +x axis with both plots showing. Watch for: the x and y readouts changing while the dot circles.

03

Two labels for one point

A Cartesian pair gives the distances of P along two perpendicular axes. A polar pair gives the distance of P from O and the angle from the +x axis. The sim places P from its polar pair like this:

From polar labels to Cartesian labels.

And the polar pair follows from the Cartesian one:

From Cartesian labels back to polar labels.

atan2 uses the signs of x and y to find the right quadrant. The sim's θ readout counts from 0° to 360°.

Key idea. The pair (r, θ) is computed from (x, y), so it is no third, independent number. Move the axes and the labels change; P stays where it is.
See itRun P with both label sets showing. Watch for: the blue and red drops lengthening and shortening while the green arm turns.
04

One circle, two sets of curves

For this motion the two descriptions are equivalent, not approximations of each other:

One motion, written twice.
  • Cartesian: x and y are two sinusoids. y is x shifted by a quarter of a cycle, so x peaks first.
  • Polar: r is a flat line at R = 1, and θ = ωt is a straight ramp.
  • The θ ramp drops back to 0 each time it reaches 2π. That is the plot wrapping the angle, not P jumping.
The four traces at ω = 1 over the 12-unit window.
See itShow only the Cartesian plots. Watch for: x(t) and y(t) both swinging between −1 and +1, a quarter cycle apart.
See itShow only the polar plots. Watch for: r(t) staying at 1.000 while θ(t) climbs and wraps.
05

Speed, period and the plot window

ω is in radians per time unit, so the speed along the circle is |v| = ωR, in length units per time unit. One turn takes T = 2π/ω.

Speed, time per turn and turns in the window.
ω

This is the sim's real ω slider: drag here and the apparatus and plots follow.

The window is tmax = 12 time units long, so it holds N = ωtmax/2π turns. At ω = 1 that is 1.91 turns. At ω = 3 it holds 5.73, so the θ plot wraps five times. At ω = 0.2 it holds only 0.38, and θ never reaches 2π.

See itSet ω to 3 and run. Watch for: x(t) and y(t) packing in nearly six cycles while the r reading stays put.
06

Polar is simpler only for the circle

Let P instead move along a straight line at constant velocity. Now x and y are each linear in t, and r and θ are not:

Computed, not simulated: the sim only runs the circle. Speed v = 1 along a line passing O at distance b = 0.5.
  • A circle about O suits (r, θ): r is fixed and θ turns steadily.
  • A straight line suits (x, y). A line through O is the reverse case: θ is fixed and r = v|t|.

Which pair is simpler depends on the path, not on which pair is more fundamental.

07

What survives a change of labels

Turning the Cartesian axes about O changes x and y. The distance from O to P is the same number in every rotated set of axes, and in polar labels it is r itself:

The distance O–P, in both systems.
Rotate the axes: x and y change, d² = x² + y² does not.
Key idea. A number every coordinate system agrees on is an invariant. In the sim, x and y swing while r stays at 1.000.
See itRun P at ω = 1.5 and read the numbers. Watch for: x and y changing from moment to moment while r holds at 1.000.
08

Where it matters

  • Radar and navigation. A radar reports range and bearing, a polar pair. The sim's scope is drawn like one, though real bearings are usually measured from north rather than from the +x axis.
  • Maps and grids. A survey grid gives eastings and northings, a Cartesian pair. The same location can be given either way.
  • Special relativity. The spacetime interval plays the same role for observers who use different coordinates: one number they all agree on.
Go deeper: why rotating the axes leaves d unchanged

Rotate the axes by an angle φ. The new components are x′ = x cos φ + y sin φ and y′ = −x sin φ + y cos φ. Then x′² + y′² = x²(cos²φ + sin²φ) + y²(sin²φ + cos²φ) + 2xy(sin φ cos φ − sin φ cos φ) = x² + y².

09

Summary

In one line. Coordinates are labels for a point. Which labels give simpler curves depends on the motion, and the distance from O to P is the same in all of them.

Key points

  • (x, y) and (r, θ) are two labellings of one point, linked by x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ.
  • On the circle, r is constant and θ = ωt, while x and y are sinusoids.
  • |v| = ωR, T = 2π/ω, and the 12-unit window holds 12ω/2π turns.
  • The distance from O to P does not depend on the axes.

Common mix-ups

  • "The θ ramp drops, so P jumps." P moves smoothly. The plot wraps θ at 2π.
  • "r is a third coordinate, extra to x and y." It is computed from them: r = √(x² + y²).
  • "Polar is the better coordinate system." It is better for a circle about O. For a straight line, Cartesian is.

Things to try on your own

  • Set ω = 2. Work out |v|, T and the number of turns in the window, then check them against section 05.
  • Pause at several moments and check that x² + y² equals r², to the rounding shown.
